- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.5) over recent days, model tends to under-forecast upward moves; adjust forecast upward by 1–2% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤ -0.5) and price is rising, model often over-anticipates; reduce forecast peak by 1–3% to avoid overshoot.
- If model shows strong upward trend after a recent spike, check for mean reversion; if sentiment turns negative, reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- If model forecast is significantly below true outcome (e.g., >5% gap) with positive sentiment, consider lagged momentum — adjust forecast to reflect recent upward momentum.
- If model over-forecasted in early period (e.g., 1–3 days) and sentiment is neutral or negative, apply downward correction to avoid “over-reaction” bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period spikes (especially after sentiment turns positive); add 0.5–1.5% buffer to final 5–7 days if sentiment is positive.
- If sentiment history shows alternating +/– signals, model tends to overfit short-term noise; smooth forecast with 3–5 day moving average if sentiment is volatile.
